However, we are fully aware of the situation in the area, as a result of correspondence, and we have been attempting to resolve the problem on an equitable basis.
The fact of the matter is that there are two groups of fishermen involved. One group represents strongly that fishermen should be permitted to fish with cod trawlers and

draggers, or more modern gear, while the other group represents that the area should be reserved exclusively for hand lining. The officials of the department have made several proposals to adjust the situation on the basis of reservation of smaller areas for hand lining. There is no prohibition contained in the fisheries regulations for Newfoundland under the Fisheries Act against fishing in these areas with gear other than that used by large trawlers. Present regulations in this regard were made effective with the full support of many of the fishermen in the areas, in order to permit full exploitation of the fisheries in the locality.

So far as this very important bill is concerned, I say to the opposition that they have failed to criticize the bill constructively and I am put in the position where I have to stand up and point out what are the real dangers in this legislation and the risks that must be taken by the government of Canada and the provincial governments in meeting these dangers.

speechtext:
The opposition have failed to realize that today not only in Canada and the United States but all through the western world and in some parts of the Asiatic world the growth of technology is so rapid and so effective that countries which were once in a deficit position with respect to food production can now look forward, if they have not already reached this point, to being surplus food producing countries.
This was the real heart of the bill, which was part of the four or five point program to get at this fundamental difficulty. We have had discussions with the secretaries in the United States, and they agree with us that our fundamental approach to this bill is sound and right. They are following an intermediate course under a new policy of raising prices on fewer units of production from each farm. In other words, they are trying to bring an end to the intensive cultivation brought about as a result of previous support policies by putting forward different policies that will reward the farmers if they produce fewer units; or in plain terms, instead of paying subsidies on the basis of acreage reduction they are now giving subsidies on the basis of unit reduction of production.
Here is the challenge before us. Can we as a nation in this twentieth century face up to a fact which has been made clear to us over the last 25 or 35 years, that technology has now outpaced the demand for food for domestic consumption and for export to such
Marginal Lands Development a degree that the level of income of farmers is being forced downward and downward, no matter how efficient they become both in production and in organizing their distribution to meet this challenge. We are in this race between technology and the finding of proper uses for land. The agricultural rehabilitation and development bill in my opinion hits at the core of this problem better than any other legislation of which I am aware, not only on this continent but in western Europe.
The bill is tied in not only with the government's accelerated marketing program, which has not only brought about greater distribution of our goods within the country but also abroad, and with some success, I might say; it is also tied in with our policy of stabilization of prices, with our policy of encouraging the organization of groups of farmers to enter into crop insurance schemes on a voluntary basis not only for cereal crops but for special crops as well. It is tied in with the main gun in our arsenal, the farm credit corporation program which will provide farmers who are on reasonably good land with the opportunity to get capital in order to make full use of that land in traditional agriculture. It is tied in with the resources for tomorrow program coming forward this fall.
I had hoped that the opposition would take this bill, discuss it in the light of these other things we are doing and ask questions as to how it would fill the gap. At the resolution stage I did my best to point out that according to the 1956 census, 120,000 farmers had incomes of less than $1,200 a year, and that this was a challenge to us to try to do something that would not only help them increase their incomes but at the same time would give an opportunity to the other 70 per cent of the farmers of Canada who are on land that can return a good living.
This is the challenge that I put before the House of Commons. I had hoped that it would inspire not only from members of the opposition but from all members a thorough discussion of what the government was trying to do and whether this was the right way to go about it. The hon. member knows that I have answered this question on two occasions during the previous debate. I repeat that in the concept in clause 4, which

relates to agreements for soil and water conservation projects, we seek to establish in all parts of Canada the same type of operation we have had under P.F.R.A. We are endeavouring to establish equality between what may be received by farmers in all parts of Canada and what has been received by those on the prairies in the last 25 years. The principles of financing will certainly follow the precedent of P.F.R.A. Under P.F.R.A. during the last two years we have been moving increasingly in the direction of joint operations between the federal and provincial governments on a 50-50 basis. This is supported by the minister of agriculture of Saskatchewan, who gave evidence before the Senate land use committee.
We have introduced what we consider is an important bill. All that hon. members of the opposition can do is snipe and ask if I have not heard of P.F.R.A. Let me tell hon. gentlemen opposite that I witnessed the birth of P.F.R.A. when it was planned by a committee composed of western members. I saw its commencement and am aware of what it can do. That legislation was endorsed and supported by hon. members who were familiar with the unfortunate circumstance of drought. It is a valuable act. If there is anything that can be said to be to the credit of the previous government in 22 years of administration it is the action taken in broadening the scope of that act. We are simply attempting to apply those broad principles all across Canada; but that is only a small portion of the value of this legislation.
There has been no discussion of the theory of alternative land use as related to markets. I have exchanged ideas on this subject with businessmen and farmers in small towns across the country. I am aware that in small towns throughout Canada groups of businessmen, professional people and farmers have gathered together to plan programs to raise the income level of farmers in those areas.
The big question confronting the government is this. Can we as a government, supported by provincial governments across Canada, move fast enough under alternative land use programs to shift that land into uses that will provide a greater return to the farmer; and, in so doing, can we move quickly enough to stay ahead of the technological process that is taking place in building up production on farms which are not marginal? That is the key issue.
If I could venture a prediction I would say that the speed with which we move will be the $64 question in terms of whether or not the program envisaged by this legislation will be successful. The question is, can governments working in co-operation gather together sufficient information quickly enough and

draft programs of alternative land use that will provide increased returns, and also keep ahead of the rising production of the good land areas and give the farmer on the good land a market for his product at a reasonable price? This has been the fundamental weakness of the price structure in agriculture for the last 20 years. To my knowledge this is the first time an effort of this kind has been made by a government in this part of the world in going out on a limb, as it were, by putting its full weight behind a program of alternative land use related to markets.

We have seen today the strong pressure which has been brought to bear in this house in respect of this measure.
I am sure this day will go down in history as being the day a minister initiated debate on third reading having already provided his own opposition. I think that represents the final step in this peculiar procedure which has taken place in respect of this bill.
I must say that we have already received as an act pamphlets advertising the minister's proposal, and in view of that fact, what has gone on here has been rather surprising to me. As a student of government I was under the impression that the wealth of the country was controlled by responsible government. In spite of the fact that this proposed bill is in the legislative process in this house, and has been introduced by the minister today for third reading, the minister has gone around the country to find opposition to it. If the minister finds no opposition in the country he can, of course, come back to this house with 200 members on the government side, and with the executives of practically all the farm organizations in existence arrayed behind him, and say there is virtually no critcism to the proposal except that expressed by members on this side of the house, which the minister can refute by saying that all farm organizations are in favour of it. I wonder, as a student of government, whether that is a legitimate form of pressure to be placed on those of us who are on the opposition side.
The minister also reminded us that we did not bring in this business regarding alternative land uses, but I think he must remember that he has given a great deal more information to the individuals with whom he spoke across the country, so far as this bill is concerned, than he has given us. He has not given us much information, or anything specific about its purposes whatsoever. I must agree with the Leader of the Opposition that we should be informed as to what is happening. Let us find out what will take place when the provinces do come into this scheme; how much money will be paid out by the federal government and how much money the provinces will have to contribute to this proposal, which is supposed to solve all of the problems of the farmers. I asked a couple of questions yesterday in respect of the farmers' union regarding this proposed bill, but as yet have not received any answers. I shall have to place questions on the order paper, hoping that in that way I will obtain some information.
The minister must have been reading different books and articles than I have read in regard to the problems of world technological

food production, because he gave a picture which indicated that the world is virtually being drowned and buried in its own food as the result of modern technology. Surely that is not a truthful position at all. I am under the impression that there are a tremendous number of people in this world who go to bed hungry every night. When I listened to the minister I began to get the impression that there is no problem, although it has been my understanding that this world food problem has not been solved at all because of a lack of imagination on the part of countries of the west, including Canada.
The area of this problem, which has not been solved, involves the devising of a means to put the food presently being produced into the mouths of the hungry peoples of the world. The problem does not involve the existence of statistical tables which show that there is an overproduction of food, but has regard to the ever increasing number of starving people in different countries of the world. There are more hungry people in this world today than there were ten years ago, and that number is increasing every year. The problem involving the destruction of world food markets by modern technological methods is a small one in terms of the world situation.
The minister suggests that great efforts must be made to increase the incomes of the many individuals on the farms who are now receiving in the neighbourhood of $1,200 per year. I admit there is a challenge in regard to raising the standard of living of those individuals, but I see no answer to that challenge in this proposed legislation. I suggest the minister should realize that those individuals are now paying, in effect, retail prices for all their needs when they should actually be paying wholesale prices. Farming is an industry, and should be entitled to wholesale prices. Perhaps the difficulty arises in many cases because the farmers are not sufficiently organized in a co-operative way to demand the privilege of purchasing at wholesale prices, but I do not find anything in this legislation in that regard.
I am sure all hon. members realize that many farms in eastern Ontario contain a great number of trees, but how can we be assured that under this legislation farmers will be able to market these trees at a better price than they are receiving today?
I fail to understand the minister's answer to the criticisms expressed by members of the opposition in respect of this legislation.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE RATES OF ALLOWANCES AND INCOME CEILINGS, ETC.
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. C-101, to amend the War Veterans Allowance Act, 1952.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I do not know of anybody in the house who would prefer to second this bill more than the Right Hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) who has been interested in veterans affairs throughout his life, particularly during all the years he has been in this House of Commons. He has consistently, year in and year out, whether in opposition or as leader of the government, pressed for attention to the veterans, and scarcely a week goes by that he does not draw to my attention some individual among our veterans population who requires special care and attention. The government generally takes the same attitude as the Prime Minister does in these matters.
I now have pleasure in bringing before the house the bill about which we talked on May 16 when we discussed at some length the resolution introducing this bill. I do not intend to repeat what I said on that occasion. I took some time then to outline the background of the war veterans allowance legislation, and to indicate the extent to which it affects veterans across this country as well as the benefits it is bringing to people who so richly deserve the thanks of their countrymen.

War Veterans Allowance Act
It is rather difficult to discuss the general principle of the bill because it contains a number of wide ranging amendments dealing with certain matters of administration and other factors. The most important aspect of the bill is, of course, the increases that are suggested in the rates and ceilings to compensate for the recognized changes that have taken place in the cost of living, and to provide for the continuation of the general relationship which has existed between the rates and ceilings under this act and pensions payable under the Pension Act.
When I was speaking on the resolution on May 16, I referred to the fact that pensions had been increased across the board by 20 per cent this year, except for the somewhat greater increase of 33 J per cent for orphaned children who had not been included in previous increases which had been made to the pensions. In giving consideration to the amount by which the rates and ceilings under the War Veterans Allowance Act should be increased, the government has concluded that the same percentage should be applied across the board as was recently granted pensioners, namely 20 per cent and that orphan children likewise should be granted an increase commensurate with those given to pension orphans. Accordingly, this bill sets forth revised schedules A and B which provide for a 20 per cent increase both in the maximum monthly rates of allowance and in the maximum total annual incomes applicable to the various classes of recipients.
I might draw your attention, Mr. Speaker, particularly to the allowances and the ceilings applicable to orphans as proposed in the schedules. The allowances are now the same as the pensions payable to one, two or three orphans respectively. The other improvement that would be proposed in the schedules is that where a recipient or his spouse is blind the income ceiling which applies is in each instance $120 a year greater than the ceiling which applies where blindness is not present. The schedules under the present act recognize the difficulty experienced by the blind to the extent of allowing a comparable increase in the income ceiling where the recipient's spouse is blind. We have thought it desirable to extend this advantage where a single recipient or a married recipient or his spouse has been thus afflicted.
The rather substantial increase in the rates and income ceilings is expected at the present time to cost about $17 million on an annual basis. This is a considerably greater increase than that which has been provided in some other years when the war veterans allowance rates were raised. In the year 1948 an increase was provided of about $3,500,000, in round numbers. In 1952, the increase was $7


million. In 1955, the increase provided was slightly over $8 million and in 1957 it was slightly over $4 million. On this occasion we are proposing to provide an increase of $17 million. That will raise the annual liability or at least it will make the annual liability quite a bit larger than it has been in the past. Just by way of comparison I might point out that the annual liability or the annual expenditure by the dominion government on war veterans allowances in the fiscal year 1956-57 -and again these figures are in round numbers-was $41 million. In 1957-58, it was just under $48 million. In the fiscal year 1958-59, it was over $54 million. In 1959-60, it rose to slightly over $57 million. In the fiscal year 1960-61 it rose to slightly over $58 million, although there was a rather substantial decrease in the number of pensioners from the earlier wars. The present proposed increase-and of course, it is an estimate-of $17 million will provide for the 20 per cent increase across the board that I have mentioned.
I shall touch on just two or three of the highlights in the bill rather than deal with it clause by clause because the intention, of course, is to do with this bill as was done with other bills dealing with veterans matters, namely to refer the bill for intensive study to the standing committee on veterans affairs. That committee will go through the bill clause by clause. Officials will be present to provide any additional information that is required by the members. Then when the bill comes back to the house, in committee of the whole house we shall again have the opportunity of discussing it clause by clause. So all that I shall do now is to touch briefly on some of the highlights in the bill beyond the ones that I have already mentioned.
Last year, as you may recall, Mr. Speaker, when the War Veterans Allowance Act was amended provision was made for the payment of an allowance outside of Canada to a qualified veteran who had resided here for at least 12 months and had left Canada as a recipient subsequent to the amendment. That has been found to be a desirable change in the act. We now propose that similar provision be made for a recipient's widow. As the act stands at the present moment, in order to qualify she would have to return to Canada if she were living abroad, and this might be a considerable hardship on a number of widows for whom return to Canada would be impractical or impossible for various reasons. We are therefore proposing that the requirement of return to Canada be withdrawn under certain conditions and therefore a widow who left Canada at about the same time as did her husband recipient in order

to live with him elsewhere, if she is otherwise eligible and if she applies within one year after his death, may become a recipient. Similar action is proposed with regard to the orphan children of the recipient so that they too will not be obliged to return to Canada in order to establish qualification.
Another highlight which affects a small but very important group of our citizens is one which has reference to South African veterans. Under this act the allowance may be given to Canadian veterans of the South African war if they require assistance. However, the deadline for service in South Africa in the present act is May 31, 1902, as that was the date on which the South African war was declared to be officially at an end. We have knowledge that late in that month there were a number of Canadian soldiers who were on board ship but who had not landed in South Africa prior to the end of the conflict. We propose granting eligibility on the service basis to soldiers who had embarked for service in South Africa prior to the deadline. There are very few survivors in this group and they are all in the 80-year or 90-year age group, so I am sure that no one would object to that type of benefit being provided.
With regard to first world war veterans, an amendment was brought before the house- I am not sure whether it was last year or the year previous-permitting them to get allowances under this act if they had been in the United Kingdom during the first world war for a period of 365 days. Similarly there were veterans of that war who were on board ship and who consequently did not get in the full quota of 365 days in the United Kingdom prior to the terminal date which was set at November 12, 1918. So we are proposing to recognize the fact that these members of the forces, in proceeding to and from the United Kingdom prior to that date, underwent hazards at sea and therefore that the time they spent on the high seas could reasonably be included in the calculation of the length of their service in the United Kingdom. If the house approves, that amendment is in the bill for consideration and I hope it will be passed.
There are other items in the bill which as far as individuals are concerned are of equal importance to the ones I have mentioned, but it is not appropriate on second reading to go into too great detail with regard to the various clauses.
The members of the war veterans allowance board, other officials of the department, my parliamentary secretary and myself and, interested hon. members in the house have put a great deal of time and attention into considering problems concerning amending the
War Veterans Allowance Act War Veterans Allowance Act. We have drawn heavily upon the useful suggestions that have been put before us by the Canadian Legion and other veterans organizations.
We have accepted most of the suggestions that have come from these organized bodies. I think the amendments we are now proposing will give recognition to changing conditions which affect veterans and their dependents and I hope the amendments we are proposing will be agreeably accepted by the great body of Canada's veterans and their dependents as well as by the people generally in our country.
The War Veterans Allowance Act, as I mentioned at the resolution stage, is designed to assist bona fide veterans who volunteered for service, in many instances endured a great deal of hardship overseas, who were lucky enough not to be wounded during the course of that service and some of whom, unfortunately, after their return to Canada, for a dozen different reasons found it rather difficult to become firmly established in civilian life and to make provision for all the hazards to which everyone is subject during the course of life.
Some of them have, through economic distress, illness within the family or for other reasons, found the going a bit difficult. To these veterans, as to the disability pensioners, there is a debt owed by the people of Canada. Once again, as with the disability pensioners, we are proposing to pay in part that debt to these men who were quite prepared, when you think about it seriously, to make the supreme sacrifice during wartime.
We hope the house will receive this bill and consider it very carefully. In committee I am prepared to give careful consideration to any suggestions which might improve the drafting which we have done here. This again, as with the Pension Act, is a subject matter to which the house can give serious attention without some of the disturbances to which we subject ourselves from time to time. My experience in the House of Commons is that when the cause of the veteran is before it, the house is quite prepared to deal with it at its best. The House of Commons, in the study of veterans legislation during the time I have been here, has always shown itself to be at its best. It is in that spirit and that mood that I present to the house this bill suggesting amendments to the War Veterans Allowance Act.

Mr. Speaker, this bill has already been discussed at considerable length in the resolution stage and I have no intention of detaining the house for more than a very few minutes at the present time.
As the minister has already indicated, this has never been a partisan matter in the

War Veterans Allowance Act house. We have all desired to do the right thing by the veterans ever since I have sat in this house. The veterans are fortunate, of course, at the present time in their minister. There are not many among my friends who managed to get into the front line in both wars. I do not know how the minister did it. I suppose he played up his age in the first war and played down his age in the second war. At any rate he managed to get into both, and if the veterans ever had a sympathetic friend, it is he.
I have no intention of dealing with the details of this bill. I am sure they will receive the sympathetic consideration that the minister mentioned. But I thought I should like, for just a moment or two, to carry the mind back and picture these men, many of them now old, who are receiving these benefits and whose minds will no doubt be carried back to the days when they made the efforts and sacrifices by which we are now seeking to deal justly.
I should like just for a moment to refer to the South African war, of which there are a few survivors left, and to recall that they were the pioneers. This was the first time we had ever sent troops overseas, and I should like to recognize their service and the example they have been ever since to others.
Then I should like to go on to the first great war. There are somewhere between
35,000	and 40,000 veterans of that war who will receive the benefits of this bill. I should like to recall the summer of 1914 and read quite briefly from the speeches of Sir Robert Borden and Sir Wilfrid Laurier in the special session of 1914 after war had been declared.
I will do this very briefly, but I have been moved by what I read here as showing the spirit of co-operation which I am sure will be most pleasant to us all. I will now read very briefly from what Sir Wilfrid Laurier said on August 19, 1914. I would ask the house to bear in mind that in 1914 we did not have to declare war ourselves; it was declared for us; but there was no hesitation on the part of the government of that day in stepping right in and taking vigorous steps to make our participation real. I am glad now to read from what Sir Wilfrid said, and I think the house will be glad to hear it:
It is our duty, more pressing upon us than all other duties, at once, on this first day of this extraordinary session of the Canadian parliament, to let Great Britain know, and to let the friends and foes of Great Britain know, that there is in Canada but one mind and one heart, and that all Canadians stand behind the mother country, conscious and proud that she has engaged in this war, not from any selfish motive, for any purpose of aggrandisement, but to maintain untarnished the honour of her name, to fulfil her obligations to her allies, to maintain her treaty obligations, and to save civilization from the unbridled lust of conquest and domination.
[Mr. Macdonnell.l
We are British subjects, and today we are face to face with the consequences which are involved in that proud fact. Long we have enjoyed the benefits of our British citizenship; today it is our duty to accept its responsibilities and its sacrifices.
Sir Robert Borden, in reply, said:
I have listened...with the utmost interest and
profound admiration to the patriotic speech which has just fallen from my right hon. friend the leader of the opposition. Already, even before parliament had been called, he had announced to his friends and to the country that his meetings were discontinued, that the voice of party strife was hushed for the time being, and that he and his friends would co-operate in every way with those upon whom falls the duty, the very responsible duty at this moment, of administering the affairs of this country-
I read that with feeling because I thought perhaps others might be interested to have that recalled to mind, and would take pleasure in the fact that at that moment we had such unanimity in a common cause.
I look back to the war of 1914, and the rather happy go lucky way, perhaps, many people went to war. I like to think of one boy who had joined up and received his first pay. In those days pay was handed out in legal tender. When this boy was handed his first pay he said, "What is this for?" He was informed that it was his pay. "My God, do we get paid to fight?" was his comment.
I remember the first big action in 1915 in which Canadians took part and distinguished themselves. Then comes that ghastly period from 1915 to 1917 when we were involved in trench warfare where men had to cross flat fields in the face of machine guns, suffering fearful casualties.
I recall the first appearance of tanks in September of 1916. One can always find a certain amount of humour even in war, and it is a fact that when these ungainly creatures, which looked liked prehistoric monsters, lurched and rolled across the battlefield, they were greeted with roars of laughter.
The battles of the Somme, Vimy Ridge and Passchendaele belong to those days. Then came the early days of 1918 when we nearly lost the whole thing and then the 100 days from August 8 to November 11, and the steady relentless march to victory.
With victory we thought we had-God forgive us-saved the world for democracy. If we had been told in 1918 that in something less than 20 years we would be faced with a much worse situation we should not have believed it. Then came the second world war and the terrible days of Dunkirk, the march across Africa, the days of El Alamein, D-day and the march through France, Italy, Belgium and finally Germany.

speakeroldname: Hon. Pierre Sevigny (Associate Minister of National Defence):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I be allowed to say a few words about this legislation. I need not tell the house that I heartily approve this bill.
Once again, these measures prove to those who served in the three armed forces during both world wars and the Korean war, that the Canadian government in fully conscious of its responsibilities towards those who, when the hour of danger struck, did not hesitate to go abroad to face the enemy, in order to preserve the principles in which they believed and an ideal which was so worth defending.
Mr. Speaker, most particularly, I should like to refer to the remarkable services rendered by our Canadian soldiers during both world wars. One thing which adds value to the heroic deeds of our Canadian soldiers in the war is the fact that this country, either in the first world war or in the second world war was never as directly threatened as France the beautiful, or even Great Britain, despite the natural barrier of the English channel in the case of the latter
On the contrary, this country's frontiers were such that no other country was better protected from the horrors of war than Canada.
Why was it, then, that so many of our people, both in 1914-18 and in 1939-45, freely accepted to don the uniform and to go abroad

to fight an enemy that did not even seem to threaten them in any direct or precise manner?
Perhaps the true reason lies in the fact that some Canadians had enough love for their respective mother countries, namely Great Britain and France, to feel compelled to lend a hand to those who had to fight for their own survival.
But, in my opinion, if so many Canadians joined the armed forces of their own free will, it is mostly because we, in Canada, are conscious of our responsibility towards democracy. We know how good it is to live freely in a free land. We also appreciate all the advantages of this extraordinary freedom we enjoy thanks to our way of life and especially to our system of government. We realize that freedom must be defended at all costs and that the ideals of truth, law and justice must be the formal rule of all of man's actions.
Moreover, I am of the opinion that the soldiers of the first world war, just like the ones of the next generation to which I belonged, namely those of the second world war, and those who fought in Korea, felt, when they signed up, that since they had the privilege of living in a free country, it was their duty to go and defend freedom on a foreign soil and to check the tide of barbarism which was threatening the whole of humanity.
I believe that the fact that Canadian soldiers volunteered to fight for this ideal makes their services even more commendable than those of the soldiers of other countries, who were fighting for their own survival. Thus I feel that we are justified to pay a special tribute to our veterans who, being the victims of their own sacrifice, must now suffer from the serious wounds sustained on the field of honour.
I feel that we have a duty to recognize and reward the services of those men by introducing, as is being done today, legislation to make their old age more bearable.
There is a second reason why our veterans deserve to be recognized in a very special way. If there is today unity between the two races forming our country, the basis of this unity can be found in the fact that Canadians of various extractions, French, English, Irish, Scottish and others, were willing in times of danger to join hands, to combine their efforts toward the same goal, the same ideal. Through their valiant deeds, they have achieved glory, but they have also made possible, for times of peace, the national unity that we are enjoying today.

This national unity that our veterans have forged in war years, at the cost of much suffering, is well worth mentioning today and time and again so as to maintain it and strengthen it in times of peace.
This bill acknowledges the merit of those soldiers of truth, justice and law who, during the critical years of the first and second world wars, fought for the survival of the ideals of democracy and liberty.
I feel the government and indeed all parties deserve special commendation for giving unanimous support to the bill now before the house.
I would not want to take more of the time of the house but I think hon. members will understand that it is because I am a veteran that, once in a while, I like to pay homage to my comrades in arms who fought with such distinction on the battlefields, to pay homage especially to those who must now carry the burden of serious wounds because they were true to their duty, and who have to rely on state assistance for a moderately comfortable existence.
Mr. Speaker, it is on their behalf that I thank all the members of this house for their support of this bill which, I am sure, will carry unanimously.

Mr. Chairman, I rise to support the requests for a further increase in the interest rates which were made by my colleagues on this side of the chamber, and also to reply to some of the arguments made by the parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Veterans Affairs last evening.
The parliamentary secretary said, as reported in yesterday's Hansard at the top of page 5634, that we should stick to the original principle. I believe the original principle was that the interest rates paid by the government on this fund should be in accord with the prevailing rates in the country as a whole.
Even if an error has been committed in the past and we have departed from that principle in the past, I see no reason why we should perpetuate that error and compound it again at this time.
The important fact is that this money is veterans' money. It belongs to the veteran and the government has had the use of it. In fact, the government has had the use of it for a number of years now at a much lower rate than the prevailing commercial rates in the country as a whole. I feel we ought not to take advantage of the veterans in this way. If the government is not prepared to pay the prevailing rates, I think they should relinquish the administration of this fund and hand it over to a special committee of veterans set up for this purpose.
Army Benevolent Fund Act
Last evening the parliamentary secretary said that the fund came first and the use came second. What difference does that make? The fact is that parliament-with the support of all parties of this house, I believe- determined that this fund should be used in this particular way. Evidence has been produced in committee that this fund is being depleted too rapidly to perform the function that parliament assigned to it, and because of that the fund will have to be revised on an actuarial basis which will give it a shorter period of usefulness, or else the yearly benefits of the fund will have to be curtailed.
Neither of these courses would be necessary if the fund was permitted to earn revenue at the prevailing commercial interest rates. The purpose of the bill which we now have before us is to remedy this situation, but we are providing only a partial remedy. It is true that we are raising the interest rates, but the increase in revenue from these higher interest rates will still leave the fund $60,000 per year short of what it requires to carry out the normal services that it has been providing down through the years.
Surely if we are going to remedy this situation we must remedy it completely, and not half do it. I believe that was the consensus of the standing committee on veterans affairs, or at least it was the opinion of the majority of that committee. Therefore I urge the government again to reconsider this matter and bring in the necessary amendment to complete the job that this bill sets out to do.

Mr. Chairman, I need hardly say that it is always with some misgivings that a newly

Supply-Secretary of State appointed minister is faced with the responsibility of introducing his estimates in the house, I shall discharge this responsibility with all the co-operation expected by the house. (Text):
I should like to make a few brief remarks with respect to the estimates of the Department of the Secretary of State. This is one of the oldest departments and I feel that most hon. members are sufficiently familiar with the operations carried on within it that it is not necessary for me to take the time of the committee to outline them.
The expenditure of the department is, as hon. members will note, just over $5 million annually. The estimated amount required to operate in the period 1961-62 is $94,117 more than that which was estimated for 1960-61, an increase of 1.8 per cent.
This department is also a revenue producing department, and I might say that the revenue for the year 1960-61 was $2,726,550, which represents a small increase, namely $28,535, or slightly more than 1 per cent over that collected in 1959-60.
I should like to indicate briefly the reasons why I am asking the committee to approve an amount of $94,417 more than the amount estimated for last year. In some areas the increase is more substantial but in others we have been able to effect certain economies, and thus the total additional amount required is relatively small.
Our salary item is up $149,167 over last year. This is almost entirely due to salary revisions, statutory increases and reclassifications, since the net increase in the department's establishment is only one position. There is also an increase of $15,000 in the amount required to provide for translation done outside the bureau for translations, and an increase of $18,000 for supplies and equipment in the nature of special types of filing and storage equipment in the companies division and the patent office.
Thus we estimate a total gross increase in our requirements for certain operations of $182,167. Against this figure we balance the economies to which I alluded earlier. The large item here is a decrease in the costs of printing patents and the Patent Office Record. We show a total decrease under our publications object of $75,800. In addition there is a decrease under other items of $12,250 which,
5666	HOUSE OF
Supply-Secretary of State when added to the decrease under publications, gives us a total figure of $88,050 less than we estimated that we required for these objects last year.
We therefore need $182,167 more than we estimated for last year for certain of our operations, and $88,050 less for others, giving us a net requirement of $94,117.
Having delivered myself of these statistics I am prepared to attempt to deal with such questions and to accept in a co-operative spirit such suggestions as hon. members may care to make as the appropriate votes are called. I would point out that the order in which it is proposed that my estimates will be dealt with is, first, the Department of the Secretary of State, then the chief electoral officer, followed by the civil service commission and finally the Department of Public Printing and Stationery. In the interest of orderly discussion I would suggest that this order be carefully followed, disposing of each branch and likewise of each vote of each branch, before passing on to the next.

Mr. Chairman, the committee is happy to welcome the new minister presenting his estimates to the committee for the first time and we wish him well in his new office. I hope-and I have repeated this for many years since 1945- that the new occupant of the post of Secretary of State will stay long enough in this post to become acquainted with this very complicated department and so that we may be in a position at a future time to be a little more difficult with him and to expect that he will be an expert in each of the branches of his department. That has been "lacune", as we say in French, in the past. As soon as the minister has been long enough in the department for hon. members to feel that they should be questioning him closely he disappears to another department or to the Senate. I do not know why the Secretary of State is picked for that particular function although if my hon. friend feels he should go to the Senate I have no objection, of course, and I would wish him well there, too.
Thank you.

As the minister has said, the Department of the Secretary of State has a number of important functions to perform. However, at this time I wish to make only a few general remarks relating to the branch dealing with patents, trade marks, copyrights and designs in a


general way because I will come back to these items for questioning more specifically during the discussion of the particular estimate.
As you know, Mr. Chairman, it has been a little bit difficult to get ready to question the minister on these estimates this afternoon because the last report which we have from this department covers the year ended March 31, 1960, and of course that is hardly useful at this late date. I do not blame the minister for this, and I was assured that if the estimates had been taken up a little later we could have had more information. However, I will try to proceed by the slower process of questioning.
As I was saying, one of the important branches of the Secretary of State's department is that which relates to patents, trade marks, copyrights and designs. It is quite some time since we received the royal commission's reports on patents, industrial designs and copyrights. One of the first questions I ask the Secretary of State is whether it is the intention of the government at this time or in the very near future to implement the reports of the royal commission or at least to take some of the suggestions from them and include them immediately in the existing acts by way of amendment.
There are two ways to proceed, of course. The first is to introduce a new patent act, a new industrial designs act and a new copyright act. The second is to take some of the suggestions in the reports already presented by the royal commission and bring them forward as amendments to the existing acts. As the house knows, these very important pieces of legislation, the Patent Act, the Trade Marks Act, the Copyright Act and the industrial designs act bring about, in a way, monopolies in favour of a particular person or company, and the departmental report has shown in the past and would show now if it were available that the owners of these so-called privileges are not in the main Canadian subjects.
In 1959-60 Canadians obtained approximately 1,500 patents out of 21,000 granted by our patent office, and the same thing can be said about trade marks, industrial designs and copyrights. In the light of the desire of the government to see that the rights of Canadians are protected, possibly something might be found in the royal commission reports on patents, industrial designs and copyrights which might be helpful.
I know, for example, that only recently in the course of the investigation into drugs being conducted by the combines investigation branch it was found that the prices of

drugs are greatly affected by patents, by the exclusive right of a certain person or company, mostly foreign, of course, which owns a patent and can dictate the price of a particular drug because they are the exclusive manufacturers and owners of the right to make that drug. It is true that there are some provisions in our Patent Act which permit licensing but these are very difficult provisions. The royal commission suggested some broadening of the licensing features with respect to patents to allow Canadian industry and the public to benefit from these inventions whether they concern drugs or other things.
In connection with the industrial design and copyright legislation there is one feature that comes to my mind. The revenue of these two branches is very low and one reason why it is so low is that the acts are not operative. We require as soon as possible a new copyright act and a new industrial designs act. They are antiquated and almost useless in their present form. If the minister will look at the figures for 1959-60, and they must be similar for 1960-61, the revenue of the industrial design branch from filing fees was $4,000 and I believe the revenue in the case of copyrights was $17,000, hardly sufficient to pay half of the cost of the salaries involved in these two branches.
But that is not the one and only reason for amending these acts. The real reason is that the acts are not operative. We need a new copyright act, one that will protect the rights of Canadians. Again, this act is being used by people who are foreign to this country to exact very high fees or royalties without any control being exercised through our own legislation except by so-called international agreements which are really designed to protect the rights of people in other countries because they are the ones who have the greatest number of copyrights.
I am simply making general remarks. I ask the minister to take a look at the legislation in the light of the three reports on patents, copyrights and industrial designs. I have not said much about industrial designs because the subject is rather technical but, as the minister knows, the present act is very faulty. It is only supposed to cover the shape, appearance and configuration of an article like a Coca-Cola bottle because it has ribs on the side or in the case of other articles the round shape or hollow shape or whatever the case may be. The act does not cover any mechanical features, and the real purpose of an industrial design patent is to cover the mechanical features which are not the subject matter of a patent of invention. I do not 90205-6-3584
Supply-Secretary of State intend to say more at this time. I think I have said enough of a general nature and I will question the minister on the particular items of his estimates as they come before us.

Here is the problem: In the light of the Ilsley report, would it be better to adapt our law to American legislation or should we keep the provisions of our Copyright Act which stipulates that copyrights are good for a period of 25 or 50 years after the writer's death? If we can thus ratify the universal convention immediately without having to amend the existing legislation, we will have the protection we need against certain provisions of American legislation which, at present, are prejudicial to some of our writers,

Mr. Chairman, I should like to make a proposal which would benefit national unity and which, if adopted, would at the same time represent a substantial saving for the government.
I would like to say a few words especially about the publication in French, of certain documents issued by parliament or the government.
Section 133 of the British North America Act, 1867, reads as follows:
Either the English or the French language may be used by any person in the debates of the houses of the parliament of Canada and of the houses of the legislature of Quebec: and both those languages shall be used in the respective records and journals of those houses; and either of those languages may be used by any person or in any pleading or process in or issuing from any court of Canada established under this act, and in or from all or any of the courts of Quebec.
The acts of the parliament of Canada and of the Legislature of Quebec shall be printed and published in both those languages.
The last paragraph of the British North America Act does not suggest any procedure, but it certainly does not recommend an English original and a French translation. It is clearly stated in the first part:
and both those languages shall be used in the respective records and journals of those houses.
It would therefore seem that the legislator intended both languages to be used equally, and not separately, by producing an original text of which a translation would be made later.
Mr. Chairman, I would like to commend this Canadian government which, for some time now, has had some of its publications printed in both languages under the same cover. I have here a bilingual report entitled:
Report of the special committee responsible for considering the proceedings of the House of Commons, jointly with the Speaker, submitted by the Hon. Roland Michener, Q.C., Speaker of the House of Commons.
which was published on July 25, 1960.
I might also point out that Votes and Proceedings, bills and all documents of the Quebec legislature are printed in both languages.

Every paper there is printed in this way, The cover is printed in both languages, i.e French and English, and the text inside is also bilingual, that is French on one side and English on the other. The order paper of the Quebec legislature follows the same pattern,
By printing first of all the English text and then the French text, we may sometimes experience delays of several days, weeks or even months, for instance in the case of minutes and proceedings of committees of this house and of the Senate. And what about annual reports of some departments?
I have here some French editions which were published two months after the English ones. In such cases, the French version is so outdated that its value is greatly reduced.
French speaking members of the house and people who wish to carry out research will rather use the English version which is available, than wait for a French translation which does not come. Those people will not go to the trouble of reading the French version when it comes, after weeks, perhaps even months, of delay, a situation which makes it practically useless.
To facilitate the consideration of this problem, let us take as an example Hansard for the House of Commons and for the Senate, bills, committee, board and departmental reports and, finally, the Canada Year Book.
I wish to point out that, as I said a while ago, there has been great improvement in that respect under the present administration. Indeed, instead of getting the minutes and proceedings of the committees of the house two, three, six and even eight months after the English version of the reports, we get them only a few days or a few weeks late.
The English and French versions of Hansard of the house and of the Senate could be printed side by side in the same edition; thus we would have only one edition with both versions, instead of two diiferent editions.
The same thing could be done for bills by printing both versions of amendments side by side, and the explanatory notes, at the bottom of corresponding pages.
That is the system which has been followed since confederation, in the legislature of the province of Quebec. As I said before, it was even tried here once, as an experiment, under the present government, with a report of the Speaker of the House of Commons.

The same thing could be done for committee reports as for bills; the English and French versions could be printed side by side. Naturally, the translation of the minutes and proceedings would have to be hurried up by giving stenographers' transcripts to the translators instead of letting them wait for the printed version. If you calculate the amount of time it takes to transcribe the stenographic reports, to revise them properly, to set them up, to print them and to prepare and distribute the booklets, then translation can easily be delayed for several weeks. If translation were done from the transcript of the shorthand notes, the French version would be available as soon as the English edition.
As for commission or departmental reports those publications are of the utmost interest to the public of both languages, and therefore they should be published not only simultaneously but in side-by-side editions.
The Canada Year Book is obviously quite extensive. It could be subdivided into several volumes with French and English pages side by side.
Mr. Chairman, coming back to reports of committees, I learned during a personal investigation, that when a Senate or House of Commons committee sits in the morning, it could be possible, like it is for Hansard in both houses, to translate and edit the text and send it to the printers within 24 hours. This would obviously involve a fast process which would require co-operation on the part of the committees, the reporters and the secretary, the translators, the editors and the printing bureau.
If the sitting of the committee ended around one o'clock, for instance, the reporter could make his copy available bit by bit as it was transcribed, instead of waiting until the whole sitting was completed. In that way, the translators could, in the afternoon, start working on the proceedings of the morning sitting, and by maintaining this rate of production, translation and revision, it would probably be possible to send the copy to the printer the following day.
This is, of course, a matter of probability, but the margin of error, even if it reached 24 hours in some cases, would be nothing as compared to the present time lag. Under present conditions, apparently, the translation is started only after the original copy has been printed and stitched. Even at that, it would certainly be possible to publish a report of committee proceedings within seven to
Supply-Secretary of State 10 days. At the present time, the French copy may weL be published only several weeks and even months, as in previous years, after the English booklet has been made available to the public.
Delegates to the last federal-provincial conference of November 1957 recall that it was possible to distribute the French text to the delegates at the same time as the English text. Of course, that was an exceptional case, but work was first sent to the translators in the afternoon; they worked until late in the night, and at nine o'clock in the morning, the French mimeographed copy was in the hands of the delegates at the same time as the English copy. This was mimeographed copy, but at the previous conference, the copy had not only been mimeographed, but printed. This shows that in the matter of translation, the French version can, if necessary, be ready a few hours after the English copy. If we want to save money and time, the next step would be to publish both versions together under the same cover, thus requiring only one setting of the type and one team working in both languages.
Mr. Chairman, there is of course the fact that a large number of committees may be sitting at the same time, both in the Senate and in the house.
One of the many problems that arise is the matter of the availability of translators. In view of that, consideration might be given to increasing the number of translators working on committee proceedings, or to having several shifts so that the work would go on without interruption.
It goes without saying that use should be made of the quickest translation facilities, and that as far as possible, the most efficient and modern methods of translation should be promoted.
Several thousand dollars would certainly be saved if there was only one printing instead of two; once the material is collected, there is only the page setting to be done, so that the French text will face the English text, and then it is ready for the press. Otherwise, there must be two type settings and two printings and everything else involved in two operations. It would also result in a saving of paper because it often happens, both in French and in English publications, that many pages are left blank. This applies not only to the official reports of the house and the Senate, but also to all committee and commission reports.

Mr. Chairman, if we examine, for instance, the figures showing expenditures incurred by the government for printing certain documents pertaining to the operation of the house and Senate, we note that in 1955-56 the English edition of Hansard cost $240,708.28 and the French edition $151,364.60, or a total of $392,072.88.
In 1956-57, the printing costs of the same documents reached $254,493.82 for the English edition, and $161,940.29 for the French edition, or a total of $416,434.11. It should be realized that those are considerable sums of money-nearly half a million dollars.
Moreover, the printing costs of the Votes and Proceedings of the house, for the same two years, amounted in 1955-56 to $13,790.66 in English, and $9,129.12 in French, or a total of $22,919.78; in 1956-57, those amounts were $16,820.20 in English, and $11,394.23 in French or a total of $28,214.43.
We could also quote similar statistics for the order paper and other documents concerning the business of the Senate and the house.
As to the minutes and proceedings and records of the various parliamentary committees, we unfortunately do not have before us separate figures for the French and English printing costs, but we have an expert's opinion on this matter, to the effect that the proportion of expenses is about 75 per cent for the English edition and 25 per cent for the French edition.
Therefore, when we say that, in 1956-57, the printing costs of the proceedings of the committee on banking and commerce amounted to $18,920.95 we may be assured that 75 per cent were spent for the publication of English text and 25 per cent in respect of the French translation. Similarly, in 1956-57, the external affairs committee asked for $10,891.02 to print its proceedings, the same proportion prevailing for the English and French editions.
Therefore those are considerable expenses representing a heavy burden on the public budget. If there is any possibility of reducing those expenses, I think we should not hesitate to do so. Indeed, printers will tell you that the main expense factor in printing is the lay-out and the time required for that operation.
Once a page, or eight, or 16 pages are all set up the press does the work. Costs are mostly made up of lay-out work. If there could be only one typesetting operation for the English

and French versions instead of two separate ones, it would result in considerable savings, in view of the large number of Hansards, proceedings and reports of committees published both by the Senate and the house in one single session. Within a few years, the savings would offset the annual cost of printing those documents.
Bearing in mind that in 1955-56, the total cost of printing committee proceedings and other documents of the house and Senate amounted to $764,429.06, including $92,607.86 for committee reports, and that in 1956-57, the same costs were $698,563.97, including $109,120.74 for the committees, one realizes the tremendous savings that would result if printing costs could be reduced perhaps 25 per cent or even more. It is not a matter of complicating the work, but on the contrary, of simplifying and reorganizing it and giving recognition to the truly bilingual character of our official documents.
Government publications are filled with tables and statistics requiring an equal number of forms in each language; in publishing a single bilingual edition, duplication of that work would be avoided.
I am only expressing a wish, but I do hope that in view of the importance of the matter from the angle of national unity, and in view of the possible savings involved, a committee of officials will soon be set up to this effect. The committee might include official representatives of the printing bureau, the bureau for translations, the editors of the various departments, as well as the secretaries of the house committees, who could jointly consider the practicality of this scheme.
The importance of publishing English and French simultaneously and side by side comes from the fact that as long as those documents are published separately, English speaking Canadians will never see the French version and vice versa, which is contrary to the spirit and the letter of our constitution. Under the present system, English texts enjoy an undeniable priority, because of the circumstances in favour of such an anomaly.
In brief, the important thing is to make sure that the French language has in fact the same rights as the English language and to see that French publications are printed at the same time as the English ones, while saving money. By publishing them side by side and under the same cover, we would

avoid this delay and we would assert the true bilingual character that is guaranteed to us by the British North America Act.

I know there must be some somewhere, for when we decided to establish a simultaneous translation system in the house, it was possible to secure the services of expert interpreters who perform a remarkable job all day long.

I wonder whether the Secretary of State should not make a serious effort to recruit translators.
On the other hand, if it is true that the translators in the employment of the government get a lower salary than those who work

for private companies, I am of the opinion that the Secretary of State should immediately put a request to the government to raise the salary of those who are particularly qualified to translate efficiently in English or in French. I support the suggestion made by the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm to intensify the efforts in that area.

I know that everybody wishes to secure the services of qualified translators, but it seems to me that someone is being lazy. They do not seem to realize the problem, and that is why I completely agree with the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm.
I hope that the present Secretary of State will do all he can and that he will hold his office long enough to enable him to complete the business undertaken, because, as the hon. member for Ottawa East (Mr. Richard) said earlier, the secretaries of state succeed each other so rapidly, these last few years, that they do not have time to complete whatever work they have undertaken. The Secretary of State would have to stay in his present position long enough, at least till the next general election. Then another one could be appointed who would prove himself very capable, and in this way such work could be continued and even increased.
Moreover, like the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm and other hon. members both French and English, I would like to see implemented in this house the system used at Quebec. The bills there are printed in two columns, one in English and one in French, which allows anyone not too familiar with the other language to follow on the translation and thus be able to better understand the legislation.
If such a system were implemented here, it could be indicated that in the event of inconsistencies the English or the French as the case may be has precedence.
Whenever there appears to be any ambiguity due perhaps to translation in either of the two official languages, it would be easy to state at the end of the bill, that the original text will have precedence over the translated version before the courts, parliament and elsewhere.
Anyhow, I am sure that the actual Secretary of State is acting in good faith and good will. As a patriot, he intends to improve the situation whenever opportunity arises, Therefore, I do not blame him in the least for the conditions which existed in the past, but I hope he will also share the views expressed by the member for Joliette-L'As-somption-Montcalm and myself.
Moreover, I have already advocated more complete bilingualism in this country. In my view, the best way would be to follow the method now in use in Quebec, that is, to print the two texts side by side so that everyone could better understand the meaning of the other.
Now, Mr. Chairman, I hope that the Secretary of State will kindly speed up the work in order to improve the situation.
Supply-Secretary of State

Mr. Chairman, I wish to thank very sincerely the hon. member for Hull (Mr. Caron) and the hon. member for Joli-ette-l'Assomption-Montcalm (Mr. Pigeon) for what they said about me, and especially for their really practical and appropriate suggestions, which I shall not fail, indeed, to take into account in carrying out my duties.
However, I should like, at the very start, to say that I wish to reply particularly to those remarks, because the problem seems to me of capital importance. For instance, I simply wish to point out, to begin with, that the jurisdiction of the Secretary of State is somewhat limited by paragraph 3 of chapter 270, dealing with the bureau for translations;
-the duties and function of which are to collaborate with and act for all departments of the public service, and both houses of the parliament of Canada and all bureaus, branches, commissions and agencies created or appointed by act of parliament, or by order of the governor in council, in making and revising all translations from one language into another of all departmental and other reports, documents, debates, bills, acts, proceedings and correspondence.
In other words, the point is that for all branches, departments and particular agencies, those branches, departments or agencies ask the bureau for translations to do such and such a task, such and such translation work; it is therefore the responsibility of the authorities of each branch or department to determine the work they want to be performed by the bureau for translations.
I must say there is, it seems 10 me, a constant improvement and that, more and more, instead of using at times the English language, and at other times the French language in those documents, at least in the very simple ones, such as letter and envelope headings, etc., the tendency is increasing to use both languages simultaneously. And I feel that even from a practical point of view much success has been achieved and that, in my opinion, is more in accordance with clause 133 of our constitution.
On the other hand, as far as the translation services are concerned, I think we have recently recommended to the civil service commission to raise the translators' salaries and the hon. member for Hull is quite right when he says we should do more along these lines in order not only to add to the number of our translators but also to increase their qualifications.
I must say that the bureau for translations has a staff of highly qualified men who perfectly discharge their duties, but we often ask quite a lot of them, more than they

Supply-Secretary of State can do, with the net result that those requirements cause delays which are not due to the bureau of translations or to the translators but rather to the fact that there are not enough translators.
On the other hand, I must say that we now experience lots of difficulties when recruiting translators. I understand that about twenty positions remain open, despite all efforts to create an interest among translators who come to the rescue of those already with the bureau who, in my opinion, do their duty perfectly well.
Now, about the department itself, and this, I think, covers the third part of the remarks made by the hon. member for Hull and the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm-I am most happy to see that cooperation as between members of the opposition and government members is achieved on such a sore point as that-I must say that we have most successfully tried to establish the idea of bilingualism at most levels of the administration of the printing bureau.
Recently we opened a shop in Toronto which, of course, comes under the Queen's printer, and the experiment has proved most fruitful, as French and English publications are found there side by side. As a matter of fact, the last report I received was astounding. It is remarkable to note the increase in the sales of French publications, simply because the French issue was put immediately beside the English one.
This might be an incentive for the citizen who wants to improve his French or English. He can buy both the French and the English editions.
Moreover, we intend to open another establishment of this kind in the very near future in Montreal, and we will proceed exactly the same way.
I must indeed say that the sales manager is perfectly bilingual.
As to the other things we have done, I might mention a few. Notices to tenderers are now completely bilingual. There is no need to change the form according to whether we are dealing with a French speaking or English speaking tenderer, because the same form is sent in both languages to all parts of Canada.
This also applies to calls for tenders, to calls for a description of machinery, to general circulars, to instructions to employees and even to bail-point pens or pencils, which previously had only an English inscription.
I should also mention some improvements for which I can take no credit, since they
[Mr Dorion.]

were brought in before I took this office, perhaps under the former administration, I do not know, and I do not want to take credit that is not mine. However, to the list I have just given, we could add the following doc-cuments:	printed specification documents,
printed specification forms, business forms, slogans on stationery items, various posters for boards, directions inside as well as outside the buildings, parking signs, press releases and the samples which are now under press.
As for the secretary of state department itself, we have moved to other quarters quite recently, and that was an opportunity to see that everything be entirely bilingual, in order to respect the principle so eloquently upheld by the hon. members for Hull and for J oliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm.
