Mr. Chairman, 1 hope that I will be forgiven if I speak in respect of a particular element of the responsibilities of the Secretary of State which has already been touched on briefly by one of my colleagues, and I refer to the matter of an amendment to the Canadian Copyright Act or, as I should like to be able to refer to it, the repeal of the present act and the institution of a completely new, modern act, as recommended by the report of the Ilsley commission and, in addition, of course, the ratification of the universal copyright convention.
I was somewhat astonished this afternoon to hear that consideration has been given by the department to the ratification of the convention prior to an amendment to the Copyright Act. Since excellent legal authority has looked at the problem and, in fact, the Ilsley commission was set up and assisted by the best authorities regarding the subject, I should like to refer to a statement made in section 6, page 16 of the report.
That statement is, that Canada, as a signatory to the convention, has a right to ratify it, but before it does so, it must be in a position, under its domestic law, to give effect to the terms of the universal copyright convention, article 10, and, therefore, it is of prime necessity that an amendment to our domestic legislation should be made first, in point of time, and, thereafter, we may ratify this convention.
That statement appears to be unopposed by anyone who appeared before the commission, and they seem to have had the best reasons for making it. In fact, the minister has been quoted earlier this year, after he received an extensive brief from the Canadian Authors

Association which recommended a new copyright act and ratification of the convention, in the Toronto Globe and Mail, as having told the president of that association that the amendment to the Copyright Act was under way now, and that it might be expected not this year, but next, but that parliament would not be asked to pass upon it at that time, and that a further year's delay might be expected while those interested individuals in Canada had the opportunity of studying it.
I should like to refer to that article appearing in the Toronto Globe and Mail of March 8, 1961, where the minister is reported as follows:
"I hope that it will be possible to introduce a bill to revise the Copyright Act at the next session of parliament," Mr. Dorion wrote. However, following the introduction of the bill, parliament may decide to stand it over to the next session, so as to afford those interested a better opportunity of studying it and expressing their views on it.
The minister then goes on to deal with the universal copyright convention.
I became interested in this subject, which is a fairly erudite one, not through my practice of law, because I have not had the opportunity, but because of a situation which arose in my own constituency. In that constituency there is a young professional man who is the author of a book, and who intended to publish that book in Canada in an effort partly to create employment for Canadians. I do not think there is any point here for me to beat a dead horse, by saying that there is considerable unemployment in Canada and has been for the past three years, but let me say that the printing and publishing industry of Canada is in pretty sad shape.
There is a provision existing in the United States copyright act providing that books must be printed and published in the United States, and, if printed here in Canada and sold in the United States, after the sale of 1,500 copies, the author loses his copyright. The effect of that provision is that any book printed and published in Canada, and sold in the United States, may be pirated after 1,500 copies have been sold.
The author to which I refer wrote his book with the anticipation of selling a considerably larger number than 1,500 copies in the United States. I expect every author has that same anticipation. Although that individual consulted several Canadian publishers both in the Niagara riding and outside, he was advised not to publish in Canada for his own sake, but to publish his book in the United States. He, accordingly, did so.
It is impossible to say, in terms of dollars and cents, how much was lost to the Canadian publishing industry as a result of
Supply-Secretary of State that one book being printed in the United States, but if we multiply the amount involved in respect of that one book, by the number of books written by Canadian authors and published in the United States, I suggest to the minister there is a very large amount lost annually, and we are not doing what is necessary to assist that industry, which is already in bad trouble. By the mere fact of assisting the publishing industry I would suggest that the minister's immediate response, when he has such a small department and only $5 million to expend, should have been as follows. One of the first things he should have done on coming to office was to insist that his departmental officials place before him and before the house for discussion a copyright act.
Because of the situation which arose in Niagara, I began to look into the situation and I found that ratification of the universal copyright convention, which was a convention mainly instigated by the United States, would have the effect that the printing requirements of the United States domestic legislation would no longer take effect and therefore Canadian authors would not be in jeopardy if they printed in Canada.
Canada was a signatory of the Berne convention and of the Rome convention. These things were discussed as well as the possibility of ratifying what had been signed at the universal copyright convention. The Ilsley commission spent a great deal of time on this matter and heard a great number of interested groups and individuals in this country. They produced the first report in 1957 which dealt only with copyright and, of course, not merely copyright in literature, music, works of art and things of that kind. It went much further and covered a much broader field than the present legislation, which I think was last amended or enacted in 1924. Surely, all hon. members will agree that since 1924 the world has changed drastically and in this time little protection has been given to authors, artists, architects and those individuals who produce musical works in this country, certainly not the protection which should have been given to them. The report which was produced by the Ilsley commission is one which starts with a new act in force and that is the copyright act introduced in the United Kingdom in 1956. It is a radical departure from our old Canadian Copyright Act. It is an easily readable act. It is a long act, and it establishes quite a few new rights.
The commission which sat in Canada had before it not only the new United Kingdom

Supply-Secretary of State act but in addition the reports of the committee in the mother of parliaments, and the report of the commission out of which the act arose. It looked into this and felt that some of those rights were not ones which should be in effect in Canada. If one spends sufficient time to read the report of the Ilsley commission on copyright one will find that in fact it is a simple document. It is one which almost goes so far as to draft the legislation.
Now, I cannot believe that in the minister's department in the past four years there could not have been found at least one person who could sit down and draw a draft act at least fully in conformity with the Ilsley report. Had this been done there then would have been an opportunity to circulate it around the country and give authors, artists and composers the opportunity to comment on something which was concrete. So far there has been no indication from this government as to whether it intends to adopt the principles of the Ilsley report, whether in fact it intends to adopt the various provisions which it recommends, or whether it intends to go off on another frolic of its own.
I think there are a lot of unpopular things which are recommended by the commission but the commission took a very bold view in order to try to produce legislation which is the right thing. I think there is a concept in the public mind that anything which is printed or published is by the common law protected and that it is an infringement of the common law to copy any such thing. Well, it does not take too much study of the subject to find that this is arrant nonsense. In the absence of a copyright act there is no natural law against using the product of any man's hands or his brains. This is the reason why jurisdictions around the world have brought in copyright acts, and have tried to keep them up to date.
Obviously, because of the nature of copyright because it is in a piece of music, a painting, a book, a scientific article, plans for a house or dwelling of some kind, because of the nature of the article, in which copyright may exist, because they are interchangeable all across the world, it therefore makes it most important that whatever our legislation be, it be something which is workable not only in Canada but around the world.
The universal copyright convention is the most modern of the agreements signed by individual countries. I believe only Russia and China did not sign. Most of the countries of the world that signed the convention


have ratified it. Some of the countries, including the United Kingdom which had entered into the Berne agreement and the Rome agreement on Canada's behalf have become members of the universal copyright convention and were able to do this only after they amended their domestic copyright legislation.
I say to the minister that if his department or his officials are of the opinion that they should ratify the convention without first bringing in a new copyright act, under the authority of the Ilsley commission's report, it would appear that we shall be pretty well stuck with the provisions of the present copyright act. The Copyright Act in force at the present time does not cover modern situations such as television, the right to televise certain material which is in copyright, the right to make records, the right to sell these. It does not cover juke boxes and the records used in them; it does not cover the type of literature which is now available but which was not available in the 1920's. It makes no provision for the changes that have occurred in the last 35 years. There has been a tremendous change in trade and a tremendous change in the speed with which these articles may be passed across the world. Television, of course, can show us now instantaneously something that is occurring elsewhere and I am told that before very long we shall have instantaneous television coverage of what is occurring on the other side of the world.
Copyright is becoming of increasing importance There are authors, artists, architects and musicians who believe that copyright should be a right in perpetuity. Of course, it cannot be that because there must be a necessary balance between what is right for the protection to a man of the fruits of his labour or of his intellect or of his skill and what is good for the body politic. At some time the ideas, the designs or the music must pass into the public domain.
We in this country are now in an unfortunate position because we do not give the necessary assistance. We not ony do not attempt to assist those creative elements in our community, we in fact depress them. We force publication in England or in the United States. In failing to protect designs, in failing to protect art and creative things of this nature we do not create a climate in which they can properly grow as they should in Canada
I think Canada is proud of its design council. Recently the Minister of Trade and Commerce brought in a new act with respect to this. Design, of course, is not copyright but the two are interrelated because if there is a copyright in an article which, is an artistic

article and which can be applied to an industrial design, then it is necessary to take away some of the copyright protections and leave them under the Industrial Designs and Union Label Act, or similar legislation,
Copyright is the first and most important of the modern legislation in the commercial and artistic fields which must come before the house, Canada cannot proceed into the 1960's in a 1920 vehicle. I would suggest to the minister that the first thing that is necessary is a crash program. I would also say to the minister that if he hears from the officials of his department that it is not possible to produce an act this year I will tell him that I as a private member in the last six weeks have almost completed producing an act. It will not be a perfect one but I have produced a draft copyright act which I will have on the order paper before the end of the session. The minister has a department where $5 million a year is spent and yet since 1957 he has not been able to produce such an act, one of the most important measures in assisting our creative people.

Mr. Chairman, I believe that this question is so important that I should like to answer the hon. member for Niagara Falls now. I thank her very much for her suggestion. I should like to note that the report on copyrights does not attempt to draft a new statute. Furthermore, the recommendations in the report have to be studied carefully before we can decide whether or not to adopt them and, if we adopt them, how to implement them.
The subject is highly complex. It took over four years in the United Kingdom following the report of their committee on copyrights before a new copyright act was adopted. I should add that we are also working on the revision of the industrial design legislation. May I add to what I said a few moments ago. Although the matter has not been decided by the cabinet yet, on the basis of legal advice we have secured I do not believe it is necessary to change our own Copyright Act in order to protect the rights of our authors. The protection to be provided in the proposed new copyright law depends on what decision is made as to the duration of the term for which protection of the copyright is afforded. I know that in the Ilsley report there is a suggestion that the period of time be changed and if we have to change the period of time it would be necessary to have a new act, but if we do not change the period of time it would be possible to adopt the last convention and protect the rights of our authors without a new act.
If the government decides to retain the present term, namely, the life of the author
Supply-Secretary of State plus 50 years, our legal advice is that the universal copyright convention can be ratified without changing our legislation. This matter is now before the government and I hope it will not be long before we will have a decision of the government in order to protect as much as possible the rights of our authors against foreign legislation which now creates a very difficult situation for them.

speechtext: Would the minister answer a question? There was an article by Miss Judith Robinson in the Toronto Telegram of January 24, 1961 in which she alleges that the minister, in attempting to protect Canadian authors, publishers and printers from American exploitation, wants it done by diplomatic representation at the international level. Her report is based on a meeting which the Secretary of State had with Ottawa printers a week before the appearance of this article in which she alleges that the minister aspires to persuade Washington at the international level to change its copyright laws to suit Canadians. This is a pretty scathing report, not unusual for the lady who wrote the article, but can the minister advise the committee whether in fact there has been some sort of consultation between his department and the appropriate authorities in the United States from the point of view of asking them to change their laws to protect Canadians?

maintopic: SCHEDULE 1. COMPARATIVE FIGURES SHOWING THE DISTRIBUTION OF THE COST OF PRINTING EVIDENCE OF VARIOUS COMMITTEES FOR THE FISCAL YEARS 1955-56 AND 1956-57,
speechtext: I might answer that this is a question which is within the authority of the Secretary of State for External Affairs, but what I said on that occasion was absolutely true. I do not know whether it is possible for me to answer for the Secretary of State for External Affairs, but the hon. member can be certain that we made every effort possible by diplomatic means in order to have that change made by the government of the United States. Even if we did not succeed, I believe it would be easier for us to follow the procedure indicated a few moments ago without being obliged to have recourse to new legislation. Surely it would be sufficient for the protection of our authors if we ratified the convention but did not accept the period of time suggested. The commission's suggestion was in conformity with the American law and we have only to establish our own law now in respect of the duration of the period of time. I believe that if we act in that way it will be possible to protect our authors.

speechtext: Yes, we fully realize that. If we ratify the convention it implies that we accept the actual period of time mentioned in our law. This is the only difficulty to my mind, but I do not believe it is necessary to refer to the American legislation to protect our own authors. I believe that the method now in existence in Canada would be sufficient in respect of the period of time for the protection of authors.

I think we should congratulate the hon. member for Niagara Falls on her clear expose with respect to the matter of copyrights. I think this whole discussion clearly raises the point that there is a conflict of opinion with respect to whether we should ratify the international convention before a new act has been adopted. The United Kingdom did pass a new act before ratifying the international convention, and I cannot see why it should be so difficult to draft an act, say for the next session of parliament, when we have had the advantage of all the work that has been done in other countries and also the work of the Ilsley commission. We have waited for a very long time for a new copyright act.
I am one of those people who is absolutely nationalist when it comes to international conventions. I know that some people in government departments are ready to seize on every international convention there is in the world and make us a party to every agreement they can make with other countries. However, we always get the poor end of the cut of beef in these matters. I have never seen us get anything very good out of an international convention. We have everything to offer others and they have nothing to offer us. This is one of those conventions where we will not get anything out of it. Others want us to agree to it because they will get something out of it. We get the short end of the stick. My point is that there is a conflict of opinion. For years, I have been asking for a new copyright act. I think we have enough material at hand now to enable us to draft a new act. It is not a question of waiting four or five years more, especially if there has been the study made during the past four years by the department as suggested by the minister.
Now, of course, the matter is rather simplified if it is true, as stated a few minutes ago, that the government has agreed the new copyright act will adopt the terms of the old act. Apparently this has been decided because it could not be changed once we

adopt the international convention. Starting from there, then, the provision of the new act ought to be a rather simple matter. I think the whole discussion has centred around the question of the term. I doubt very much that we should adopt the term in the old act without some closer study, in the light of modem conditions.

Mr. Chairman, before the item passes I should like to ask the minister a technical question. I am wondering how the department functions, and how effective it is in its relations with all its branches. There is the electoral office, the civil service commission, the printing bureau and the secretary of state department, all of which appear to me to be separate and not in any way related to the office of the Secretary of State. I am wondering how these matters are handled, in a physical sense. How do you handle each one of these departments? Is there a set-up under which a deputy minister heads each one of these departments or is this a field in which we should revise the procedure for dealing with these branches? These branches, for instance, appear to me to have very little relationship to the printing bureau or to each other.
Is it now time for some reform of these branches to facilitate the handling of them within the department? Is there something that could be done to make it easier? It

seems to me they are not related, and I am wondering if this produces some difficulty for the department?

speechtext: The functions of the translation bureau are provided by law. They are to translate from French to English or from English to French, as well as foreign languages, for all departments, parliamentary reports, documents, debates, bills, acts, proceedings and correspondence. Then too, the division is responsible for the simultaneous interpretation of speeches in the House of Commons and the publication of terminological bulletins.

Are these facilities available to members of parliament? Quite often members who are not bilingual require translations of letters that are written in languages other than French or English. Is it part of the function of this bureau to supply this service to members of the House of Commons? If so, is there any specific way in which this service is obtained?
The problem, as I understand it, has been that translations have been done by several branches for members of parliament. This
Supply-Secretary of State service is on a request basis and at the discretion of the bureau. If they wish to do it, they do so and if they do not wish to do it they do not have to do so. It seems to me that the system we have now of asking the various agencies to do this work could be greatly improved. Members should be instructed as to where this work can be done, not only in so far as the French and English languages are concerned but other languages as well. At various times, the problem is rather acute, especially when we receive letters in Croatian or some of the Scandinavian languages. It is very difficult to have those letters translated here. I am wondering if this service is available to members?

maintopic: SCHEDULE 1. COMPARATIVE FIGURES SHOWING THE DISTRIBUTION OF THE COST OF PRINTING EVIDENCE OF VARIOUS COMMITTEES FOR THE FISCAL YEARS 1955-56 AND 1956-57,
speechtext: The members of the house can have translations made by the bureau, but the bureau has to communicate with the Clerk of the house. It is to the house that the bureau is responsible, and not to each member. If there is some complaint about it, these complaints are supposed to be made to the Speaker of the House. We depend on representations from the Speaker or from the house and not from individual members of the house. Generally speaking, the translators are always ready to do whatever they are asked to do for every hon. member, even if we are not proceeding strictly in conformity with the rules and the law. The law is that we are responsible to the house and that we are obliged to give our services to the House of Commons.

Does this mean that if we wish translations to be done, we should send them through the Clerk of the house or is there an office to which we can send them? It seems to me that this procedure will be giving the Clerk of the house some unnecessary work as he would immediately be obliged to dispatch them anyway. I am not asking that this be done right now. However, I think this matter could be taken up with the Secretary of State and the Clerk of the house so that an arrangement that is understood by everyone could be worked out.
As the situation stands now, the problem is this and I am quite sure that every hon. member is aware of it. Everybody gets translations done in a different department. One hon. member finds a friend in one department, and can send his letters there for translation; another hon. member finds a friend in another department. I would suggest that there is not any formal method now by which this work can be done. If this bureau is charged with doing this work on behalf of the Clerk, possibly a better arrangement can be arrived at so that a more suitable way can be found of doing this work than

Supply-Secretary of State is at present in operation. I am not suggesting that I be told about this matter now. However, I am suggesting that the minister give consideration to discussing it with the Clerk so that study can be given to the matter with a view to working out a method which will make it a little bit easier for those of us who are not bilingual to handle some of the correspondence that is of that nature.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: SCHEDULE 1. COMPARATIVE FIGURES SHOWING THE DISTRIBUTION OF THE COST OF PRINTING EVIDENCE OF VARIOUS COMMITTEES FOR THE FISCAL YEARS 1955-56 AND 1956-57,
speechtext:
Would the minister care to comment on this department? I am particularly concerned with the changes that have been made recently on, I would suggest, a partisan basis. I will use the example of my own riding where the returning officer over a period of years has been one person. He has established a very good record. I am not sure what his politics were and I do not really care. However, he did an exceptionally good job in two elections with which I had something to do. In one of those elections we had, as I suggest to any hon. member who may not have gone through this experience, a very unfortunate occurrence that happens occasionally. I refer to a recount. A recount is very tough on the people involved having regard to the fact that it takes some time. However, it gives one the opportunity to examine the work the electoral officer has done or the returning officer has done in that area, as you have the opportunity to see the results of the instruction that was given to the deputy returning officers under his control as well as to the clerks and other officials of the returning officer.
In this particular case, to use my own vote as an example, in 1957 before the recount I had a majority of 46. After 21,000 votes had been counted I had a majority of 40. This result would strike me as being an exceptionally good recommendation for the work

of that returning officer, having regard to the fact that he was able to conduct, through the people he appointed, an election as to which, after a judicial inquiry and personal examination of every ballot in the ballot box and of the work and the reports in those ballot boxes, out of over 20,000 votes the recount resulted in a change of only six votes.
In this particular case I fail to see why that man should be replaced by somebody else, as I suggest, possibly on a patronage basis. The other gentleman in this case had been doing this type of work in a provincial field and had been very unsuccessful in it. His record was not nearly as good in the provincial field and terrific complaints were made of the enumeration and some of the other things under his jurisdiction. Now we find that, for no particular reason, unless it would be a political one, this gentleman of whom I certainly have no knowledge politically, is removed and replaced by somebody else.
It seems to me that this is one field that is of the utmost importance to us. No matter what political party one may come from, I think this statement applies to the politicians involved. However, it reflects much more on the general public and on the success that may attend our desire to see that democracy works to its full extent by having as large a vote as possible. This result hinges partly on the returning officer and the ability he shows in choosing people who will see to it that the largest number possible are enumerated, particularly in an urban area and that all citizens have an opportunity to exercise their right to vote.
We know that in rural areas a person who is not on the enumerator's list, can be put on it very easily on election day. But I agree with many of the people in my riding who will say that they will not be sworn in on election day in an area in which they have lived for 40 or 50 years. Many of them have held municipal office and have lived all their lives in that particular area. To be left off the voters' list on election day is, to them, an insult. In my particular case, the experience I have had in the elections is greater than my years in parliament would indicate. I have been closely connected with the election machinery since 1947. I have had the opportunity to observe the work of various returning officers. I have found some to be conscientious and follow the book to the letter. These people do an excellent job; I am sure they have not become mixed up in politics and politics have not been used in their cases. I would not say that politics were not

used in their appointments in the first place, but this is not indicated in their operation of this office.
On the other hand, I have seen other returning officers who in my opinion have done a very poor job. They have hired people who will go down a block and not do the job properly. I remember one particular case where a boarding house was concerned. This boarding house had 66 people in it and the deputy returning officer only obtained the names of the man and woman who owned the boarding house because he believed the rest of the people did not vote the same way as they did.
In my opinion this does not do anything for the democratic process and I should like an explanation of this from the minister. I think other hon. members may be interested in this question also. In the case of men who have proven their ability and knowledge in relation to the whole of the Canada Elections Act and the operation of it-and certainly in the case where a man has proven before a judicial investigation that he has this ability and where I think it would be safe to say that no political complaint has been made of his impartiality-why should they be replaced and somebody else put in the job where the charge of it being a political appointment could be made against that person?
As I have said on other occasions where this has been done, it seems to me it does little to advance the interests of a particular political party. I say this because one man is appointed and there may be 20 who think they should have been appointed. Only one man will be grateful for the appointment and 19 will be rather upset. It does seem to me this does not do a great deal toward accomplishing the end which is intended.
I think the average Canadian citizen is more interested in honesty, integrity and the utmost attention by people concerned so that they may exercise their democratic right, be on the voters' list and may get out on election day and exercise their franchise. They would rather have this than the old, narrow concept of getting people out to the polls to vote a particular way. We, as politicians, will I am sure look after that aspect of the matter. We will be interested in getting those people to the polls whom we want to get there. Each one of us will be doing that for his political party.
It seems to me this is not the function or even part of the function of the returning officer. I am curious about this. Out of the 265 ridings in Canada, how many have been changed since the last election, and what are the reasons for any changes that have been made?
Supply-Secretary of State
Specifically I should like to know why the change has been made in my own riding, where I think it would be very difficult for anybody to accuse the previous returning officer of having been political in any sense of the word. His job is that of clerk of a large municipality. He has the staff, the facilities and the knowledge to carry out this job and it seems to me rather foolish to change that set-up when it has worked satisfactorily.
I am curious to know how many changes there have been. Of course, none of them has been changed for political reasons; we all know that. However, I should like to know how many have been changed because of unsatisfactory service, and why has the one in my riding been changed?

First of all, Mr. Chairman, the answer to the question of the hon. member is this. Under section 8 of the Canada Elections Act, which section I believe was adopted without alteration after careful discussion in committee before coming before the house, these men are appointed on this basis:
The offices of all returning officers appointed prior to the passing of this act shall be deemed to be vacant and the governor in council may appoint-
The governor in council has the responsibility:
-to such offices either the same persons as now hold them, any of such persons or any other persons: he may also thereafter appoint from time to time a returning officer for any new electoral district and a new returning officer for any electoral district in which the office of returning officer becomes vacant, within the meaning of subsection (2).
This is the law, and I believe this section was adopted without discussion on third reading of the bill. If a complaint is to be made against a returning officer, section 58 (2) of the act applies. This section says:
Every candidate at any election and every official agent of any candidate has the right to send to the chief electoral officer in writing any complaint he may have to make with respect to the conduct of the election or of any election officer, and to suggest any such changes or improvements in the law as he may consider desirable; every such complaint or statement shall be included by the chief electoral officer in his next following report to the Speaker of the House of Commons, with such recommendations, if any, as he may see fit to make thereon.
In reply to the question put at the end of the observations of the hon. member, of all the persons appointed to date as returning officers, 81 acted as such at the 1958 general election; of this number 36 had also acted as such at the 1957 general election.
